title: Lose, and Lose, and Lose, and Win
gist: Insurgent parties win by spending years building cadre and doctrine in the wilderness, then filling the vacuum when a mainstream party collapses, as with the Bolsheviks, Republicans of 1854 and today's DSA and Trump. Brazil's Mission Party, fourth with 2.2%, is playing the same long game.

insights.claim: Successful insurgent political parties typically spend a long period in the wilderness building internal infrastructure, cadre and doctrine, marginalized from respectable politics, then fill the vacuum when a big segment of the mainstream suffers a sharp collapse.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Use as a model for spotting which political movements are positioned to capture power after an establishment collapse.
insights.locator: There have been plenty of insurgent political parties

insights.claim: Collapse timing cannot be predicted precisely because it hinges on particular individuals, so insurgents' correct strategy is to build readiness rather than time the moment.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Do not trade a political regime change on a date; monitor which organizations are prepared if it arrives.
insights.locator: What does this mean for an insurgent party's strategy?

insights.claim: When the vacuum opens it is filled by whoever has the best mix of pre-existing infrastructure, skill at navigating the moment's intrigues, and willingness to take critical risks, which can be a disciplined vanguard like Lenin's or an opportunistic outsider like Trump.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Power transitions reward readiness and nerve, not necessarily ideology or planning.
insights.quote: But the vacuum will be filled. You want to be in a position to fill it.

insights.claim: Russian Marxists organized from 1883, played a minor role in the 1905 revolution, and by 1917 the Bolsheviks maneuvered to lead the rioters and mutineers when the Tsarist regime collapsed under World War I strain.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: The canonical case of a decades-long insurgent build-up paying off at a collapse.
insights.locator: The most famous example is the Russian Communists

insights.claim: The US anti-slavery party lineage ran from the Liberty Party (1841) to the Free Soil Party (1848) and into the Republican Party after the Kansas-Nebraska Act broke the Whig Party in 1854, supplying figures like Salmon P. Chase and Charles Sumner.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Shows US precedent for a minor party's cadre becoming a major party after a coalition shatters.
insights.locator: In America, the most important case

insights.claim: The Young Turks, British Labour, the Nazi Party and de Gaulle's Fifth Republic are cited as further cases of insurgents filling a vacuum after a ruling order decomposed.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Pattern is cross-era and cross-regime, supporting its use as a base-rate heuristic.

insights.claim: Collapses were contingent: had Biden's health held, had Asquith and Lloyd George kept their rivalry in check, or had Pierce not backed Kansas-Nebraska, those collapses could have been delayed by years or longer.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Individual-level contingency is the main source of timing uncertainty in political regime shifts.
insights.locator: You can sometimes foresee the collapse

insights.claim: The Democratic Socialists of America, reorganized around Bernie Sanders supporters in 2016, quintupled membership by 2017, left the Socialist International, sent its first members to Congress in 2018, and has acted as an insurgent caucus building cadre, doctrine and get-out-the-vote capacity.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: DSA is the organized insurgent to watch inside the Democratic Party.
insights.locator: The Democratic Party's old political machine is being gradually supplanted

insights.claim: The author argues the mainstream Democratic machine collapsed, with its liberal ideology jettisoned in 2020 and its internal legitimacy lost in 2024 after campaigning for Biden then swapping in Kamala Harris, and that much of the DSA platform has since been adopted by mainstream Democratic candidates for top offices.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Expect Democratic policy platforms to drift toward DSA positions; relevant for taxation, spending and regulation risk.
insights.locator: At first the mainstream Democratic machine cast them as disreputable radicals

insights.claim: Zohran Mamdani's victory as New York City Mayor over Andrew Cuomo and Eric Adams is cited as the DSA's signature electoral success, against a local machine that imploded even more drastically than the national one.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: NYC policy under a DSA-aligned mayor is a live test of the insurgent platform in governance.

insights.claim: The conservative Republican Party collapsed by the 2016 primary, but no organized insurgent right-wing faction was ready, because existing factions were built as subservient parts of the conservative coalition and lacked an ideology justifying rule.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Explains why the right's vacuum was filled by a person rather than an organization.
insights.locator: A few years before the old liberal Democratic Party collapsed

insights.claim: Donald Trump personally filled the Republican vacuum; lack of cadre made his first term almost completely ineffective, and by the second term the MAGA coalition is more orderly and can pursue bureaucratic goals, though it still lacks interpersonal and ideological cohesion.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: MAGA execution capacity has improved but cohesion risk remains, so watch for internal fractures.

insights.claim: Brazil's Mission Party candidate Renan Santos finished fourth in the presidential election with 2.6 million votes (2.2%), and the party kept its single federal legislative seat without adding any.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Brazil's insurgent right-libertarian movement is still marginal electorally after twelve years of campaigning.

insights.claim: The Mission Party grew out of mass protests against Dilma Rousseff's corruption and is now doing the trial-and-error work of building cadre, doctrine and mass mobilization, which the author views as the correct move for an insurgent.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Treat as an option on a future Brazilian political shock rather than a near-term electoral force.
insights.quote: lose, and lose, and lose, and win

insights.claim: The Brazilian run-off pits 80-year-old incumbent Lula against Flavio Bolsonaro, with Jair Bolsonaro under house arrest and disqualified; neither is widely beloved, and the author suggests the party machines may fail in the not-too-distant future, opening space for the Mission Party.
insights.speaker: Ben Landau-Taylor
insights.so_what: Brazilian political risk is elevated by weak, aging establishment candidates; monitor for machine breakdown.
